arXiv:2409.03859v1 [math.AG] 05 Sep 2024

Fixed point counts and motivic invariants of bow varieties of affine type A

Ádám Gyenge Address: Budapest University of Technology and Economics, Department of Algebra and Geometry, Institute of Mathematics, Műegyetem rakpart 3, H-1111, Budapest, Hungary Email address: gyenge.adam@ttk.bme.hu and Richárd Rimányi Address: University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, NC, USA Email address: rimanyi@email.unc.edu
Abstract.

The class of spaces known as Cherkis bow varieties includes Nakajima quiver varieties and exhibits several favorable properties, such as being closed under 3d mirror symmetry. In this paper, we derive formulas for the generating series of the Euler numbers of bow varieties and explore their modularity in certain cases. We prove combinatorial expressions for the equivariant K-theory class of the tangent spaces at torus fixed points. We identify a subclass of bow varieties that includes quiver varieties and Zastava spaces, sharing advantageous features like the absence of odd cohomology. For these quiver-like varieties, we refine the motivic enumeration series, extending results of Nakajima and Yoshioka. Furthermore, we introduce a parabolic variant of Nekrasov’s partition function and show how it relates to the classical partition function.

Key words and phrases: 
bow variety, torus fixed point, generating series, equivariant K-theory
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14D20; Secondary 14D21, 16G20

1. Introduction

Cherkis bow varieties of affine type A^\hat{A} were originally introduced as an ADHM-type construction to describe moduli spaces of Yang-Mills instantons on ALF spaces, such as the Taub-NUT space, that are equivariant under a cyclic ℤ/m​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}-action [5]. Subsequently, Nakajima and Takayama provided an algebro-geometric description of these bow varieties using quivers [18]. These varieties are algebraic with hyper-Kähler structures on their regular loci. In the algebraic setting, they are conjectured to correspond to moduli spaces of equivariant parabolic framed torsion-free sheaves on the projective plane blown up at a point.

Bow varieties are associated to a combinatorial object called brane diagram, which consists of mm NS5 branes and nn D5 branes, along with a set of integers referred to as dimensions and local charges. The varieties are naturally equipped with a torus action that has finitely many fixed points. Combinatorial descriptions of these fixed points were provided in [17] using generalized Maya diagrams, and in [21, Appendix A] using tie diagrams.

The enumerative geometry of bow varieties was initiated in [21], where the focus was on characteristic classes (called stable envelopes) in the finite type A case. The expected 3d mirror symmetry property of these characteristic classes was later proven in [4]. While type A bow varieties are significant, the truly important moduli spaces, such as Hilbert schemes or moduli spaces of torsion-free framed sheaves, are bow varieties of affine type A^\hat{A}.

In this paper, we study bow varieties of affine type A^\hat{A} and aim to perform instanton counting by computing various motivic invariants of naturally occurring infinite sequences of bow varieties. Our first result concerns the Euler characteristic as a motivic invariant, and we obtain the following theorem.

Theorem 1.1 (Theorem 5.7).

Let e∈ℤne\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} and f∈ℤmf\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{m} be fixed vectors. Together with an additional dimension parameter d∈ℤ≥0d\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0} they determine a bow variety ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}(d,e,f). We have

∑d=0∞χ⁡(ℳ⁡(d,e,f))​qd=(∑c∈ℤn×m∑jci​j=ei∑ici​j=fjq∑i,jci​j​(ci​j−1)/2)⋅∏l=1∞(11−ql)n​m.\sum_{d=0}^{\infty}\chi(\mathcal{M}(d,e,f))q^{d}=\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n\times m}\\ \sum_{j}c_{ij}=e_{i}\\ \sum_{i}c_{ij}=f_{j}\end{subarray}}q^{\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}(c_{ij}-1)/2}\right)\cdot\prod_{l=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{1-q^{l}}\right)^{nm}.

The appearance of contingency tables cc, which are integer matrices with prescribed row and column sums, is noteworthy. These tables are fundamental objects in both enumerative combinatorics [1] and statistics [14]. In the summation, the qq-exponent is quadratic, resembling a squared distance. This observation identifies Z⁡(q)Z(q) as a (shifted) lattice theta function, aligning with the physical expectation that instanton counts exhibit modular properties. In the Appendix, authored by G. Harcos, we establish the specific modularity for a particular example.

In the remainder of the paper, we begin the study of Białynicki-Birula decompositions of bow varieties and the resulting motivic enumerations, leading to a (q,t)(q,t)-generalization of the qq-count in Theorem 1.1.

Such enumerations, containing substantial birational [2] or motivic information [20, 9], are already known for the subclass of Nakajima quiver varieties. However, extending these results to bow varieties reveals unexpected complexities. Bow varieties are not as ‘perfect’ as Nakajima quiver varieties—or, depending on one’s perspective, they possess richer motivic structures. For instance, unlike quiver varieties, the union of Białynicki-Birula cells does not generally cover the entire variety ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}(d,e,f). Additionally, in contrast to quiver varieties, bow varieties may exhibit odd cohomology groups.

Hence, as a preparation for refined counting formulas, we give detailed geometric and combinatorial analysis of bow varieties, as follows.

First, following Witten’s arguments [23], we provide a combinatorial characterization of quiver varieties within the broader class of bow varieties. Specifically, this characterization requires that the vector e∈ℤne\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} of D5 local charges be an mm-bounded non-decreasing sequence of integers:

e1≤e2≤⋯≤en≤e1+m.e_{1}\leq e_{2}\leq\dots\leq e_{n}\leq e_{1}+m.

Second, we present two combinatorial descriptions of the equivariant K-theory class of the tangent space Tx​ℳT_{x}\mathcal{M}, where xx is a torus fixed point on the bow variety ℳ\mathcal{M}. These descriptions are given in Theorems 6.8 and 6.10, which constitute a significant portion of our paper and are among our main results. We believe these theorems will be essential for future geometric studies of instanton moduli spaces. One description uses extended Young diagrams, which generalize the combinatorics typically associated with quiver varieties, while the other uses the combinatorics of Maya diagrams.

Third, we observe that the brane diagram of any bow variety can be transformed into that of a quiver variety through a combinatorial operation we call D5-swap. We study the geometric implications of the D5-swap on bow varieties. From the physics perspective, a D5-swap is often (but not always) seen as an innocent transformation that does not alter the underlying theory. Mathematically, a D5-swap can be either a benign change (such as a homotopy equivalence) or a more substantial one. For instance, the fixed point count remains unchanged under D5-swaps (Fig. 2), and our Theorem 6.11 explains that a D5-swap resembles a situation in which one variety is a fibration over the other. However, sharper statements are not generally expected, as demonstrated by counterexamples in [11].

Fourth, for quiver varieties, the Białynicki-Birula cell decomposition induced by a natural one-parameter subgroup covers the entire variety. We provide a necessary and, conjecturally, also sufficient condition for the analogous cell decomposition to cover a bow variety. The condition is that the local charge vector ee must be an m+1m+1 bounded non-decreasing sequence of integers, a relaxation of the condition that would otherwise classify the bow variety as a quiver variety. This identifies an interesting sub-class of quiver-like bow varieties.

After these preparations we can state and prove a refinement of the Euler characteristic computation to motivic expressions and virtual Poincaré polynomials, in certain cases. For example, we obtain

Theorem 1.2 (Theorem 7.5, Corollary 7.7).

Let m=1m=1 and nn arbitrary.

  • •

    The Poincaré polynomial of the (−)(-)-cells of ℳ=ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}(d,e,f) can be expressed as

    Pt−​(ℳ)=∑(B1,…,Bn)∏β=1nt2​(n​|Yβ|−β​l​(Yβ)+∑1≤α<β(|eβ−eα−1|2)CLOSEP^{-}_{t}(\mathcal{M})=\sum_{(B_{1},\dots,B_{n})}\prod_{\beta=1}^{n}t^{2(n|Y_{\beta}|-\beta l(Y_{\beta})+\sum_{1\leq\alpha<\beta}\binom{|e_{\beta}-e_{\alpha}-1|}{2}}

    where the summation runs over nn-tuples of extended Young diagrams (B1,…,Bn)(B_{1},\dots,B_{n}) with dd fixed, (Y1,…,Yn)(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n}) are their classical parts and l⁡(Yi)l(Y_{i}) is the number of columns of YiY_{i}.

  • •

    For certain integers A⁡(e),B⁡(e)A(e),B(e) we have

    ∑d≥0Pt−​(ℳ⁡(d,e,f))​qd=qA⁡(e)⋅t2​B​(e)⋅∏i=1n∏l≥1∞11−t2​(n​l−i)​ql,\sum_{d\geq 0}P^{-}_{t}(\mathcal{M}(d,e,f))q^{d}=q^{A(e)}\cdot t^{2B(e)}\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{l\geq 1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1-t^{2(nl-i)}q^{l}},

    where Pt−P^{-}_{t} counts virtual Betti numbers arising from the negative weights for a one-parameter subgroup of the torus.

Similarly, we derive formulas for the case when n=1n=1 and mm is arbitrary (see Proposition 7.11), and examples when n,m>1n,m>1. Additionally, we prove that no product formula exists for the (+)(+) or (−)(-)-Poincaré polynomials when both n>1n>1 and m>1m>1 (see Corollary 7.15), thereby resolving a question that was open even for quiver varieties. If the bow variety is quiver-like, the result is even stronger:

Theorem 1.3 (Theorem 7.17).

Assume that e∈ℤne\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} is an m+1m+1-bounded non-decreasing sequence, that is

e1≤e2≤⋯≤en≤e1+m+1.e_{1}\leq e_{2}\leq\dots\leq e_{n}\leq e_{1}+m+1.

Then the Białynicki-Birula (+)(+)-cells cover ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}(d,e,f) for any d∈ℤ≥0d\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0} and f∈ℤmf\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{m}. In particular, Theorem 1.2 gives the Poincaré polynomial of a retract of ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}(d,e,f).

Furthermore, we establish results concerning the equivariant homology groups in the special case of m=1m=1, known also as Zastavas. We relate the bow variety analogs of Nekrasov partition functions to those of the quiver variety M⁡(r,n)M(r,n)—the moduli space parametrizing rank rr torsion-free framed sheaves on the projective plane with second Chern number nn.

Corollary 1.4 (Corollary 8.3).

Let m=1m=1. Assume that e∈ℤne\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} is a 22-bounded non-decreasing sequence. Then for any d∈ℤ≥0d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0},

Z⁡(ε1,ε2,a,q)=ZM⁡(r,n)​(ε1,ε2,a+ε1​e,q)⋅∏1≤α,β≤n(s1,s2)∈Rα,βeα,eβ1s1​ε1+s2​ε2+aβ−aα.Z(\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2},a,q)=Z^{M(r,n)}(\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2},a+\varepsilon_{1}e,q)\cdot\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq\alpha,\beta\leq n\\ (s_{1},s_{2})\in R^{e_{\alpha},e_{\beta}}_{\alpha,\beta}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{s_{1}\varepsilon_{1}+s_{2}\varepsilon_{2}+a_{\beta}-a_{\alpha}}.

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. In Section 2 we recall the definition of brane diagrams and the construction of bow varieties in affine type A^\hat{A}. Section 3 explores a torus action on bow varieties and its fixed points. We provide a combinatorial condition for a bow variety to be a quiver variety and investigate the effect of swapping D5 branes in Section 4. We introduce a core-quotient decomposition for fixed point count, obtain results on generating series of Euler numbers, and prove Theorem 1.1 in Section 5. Section 6 discusses the equivariant K-theory of the tangent spaces at the torus fixed points and establishes the crucial Theorems 6.8 and 6.10. We analyze the BB cells and prove Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 in Section 7. In Section 8 we introduce the parabolic partition function associated with bow varieties and deduce Corollary 1.4. Appendix A shows that one of our fixed point count generating series is modular, and it also reveals connections to concepts of number theory (the sum-of-divisors function, theta functions).

2. Brane diagrams and bow varieties of type A^\hat{A}

In this section we recall the combinatorics of brane diagrams and the associated Cherkis bow varieties of type A^\hat{A}, as defined in [18, Section 2.2]. We follow the notation of [21, Section 3.1], but add another ℂ∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*} action, and make a few minor notation changes. Familiarity with these two papers may be helpful for the reader.

2.1. Brane diagrams, Hanany-Witten transition

A brane diagram of type A^\hat{A} (or affine type AA) is a circle decorated with some line segments which are slanted either from left to right (these called NS5 branes: F1,F2,…,FmF_{1},F_{2},\ldots,F_{m}), or from right to left (these are called D5 branes: E1,E2,…,EnE_{1},E_{2},\ldots,E_{n}). The 5-branes partition the circle into segments called D3 branes. Each D3 brane is decorated with an integer dsd_{s}, its multiplicity or dimension. (Only non-negative multiplicities will be relevant geometrically, but it is combinatorially convenient to permit integers.)

In our figures we will put the 5-branes on the ‘top arc’ of the circle; this way left and right has a meaning. An upper ++ (respectively −-) index of a 5-brane will refer to the D3 brane on its right, respectively left, see

Definition 2.1.

Assume d2+d2′=d1+d3+1d_{2}+d^{\prime}_{2}=d_{1}+d_{3}+1. Carrying out the local change

(in either direction) in a brane diagram is called a Hanany-Witten transition.

Both of the diagrams

are Hanany-Witten equivalent to the one above.

Theorem 2.2 ([18]).

For a generic choice of stability condition the variety ℳ\mathcal{M} is smooth and has a holomorphic symplectic structure. Bow varieties associated with Hanany-Witten equivalent diagrams are isomorphic.

In this paper we consider bow varieties almost exclusively with generic stability condition.

Example 2.3.

For n=m=1n=m=1 the associated bow variety (if not empty) is the Hilbert scheme of certain number of points on the plane. For example for d0=11,d1=14d_{0}=11,d_{1}=14, or for d0=d1=8d_{0}=d_{1}=8 the bow variety is (ℂ2)[8]({\mathbb{C}}^{2})^{[8]}, cf. Example 2.7

Example 2.4.

The bow variety of the example in Section 2.1 is a smooth holomorphic symplectic variety of dimension 10. It has a (ℂ∗)3×ℂt1∗×ℂt2∗({\mathbb{C}}^{*})^{3}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*}_{t_{1}}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*}_{t_{2}} torus action (see Section 3 below) with 13 fixed points.

2.3. Brane diagrams in standard form

By a sequence of Hanany-Witten transitions we may rearrange the brane diagram to the following standard form: on the top arc of the circle the NS5 branes are on the left, and the D5 branes are on the right. For such a brane diagram let us call the 5-branes, from left to right

F1,F2,…,Fm−1,Fm,E1,E2,…,En−1,En.F_{1},F_{2},\ldots,F_{m-1},F_{m},E_{1},E_{2},\ldots,E_{n-1},E_{n}.

and define the following integers (‘local brane charges’):

ei=dEi+−dEi−,fj=dFj−−dFj+,e_{i}=d_{E_{i}^{+}}-d_{E_{i}^{-}},\qquad\qquad f_{j}=d_{F_{j}^{-}}-d_{F_{j}^{+}},

and denote the multiplicity of the D3 brane in between FmF_{m} and E1E_{1} by d0d_{0}, or simply by dd.

Clearly we have ∑iei=∑jfj\sum_{i}e_{i}=\sum_{j}f_{j}, and the vectors e,fe,f together with the number dd determine all multiplicities. We will call this brane diagram “(d,e,f)(d,e,f) standard diagram”, and the associated bow variety we denote by ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}(d,e,f).

We introduce two types of moves on triples (d,e,f)(d,e,f):

[move-1] (d,e,f)↦((d+e1,(e2,e3,…,en,e1+m),(f1+1,f2+1,…,fm+1))CLOSE,(d,e,f)\mapsto((d+e_{1},(e_{2},e_{3},\ldots,e_{n},e_{1}+m),(f_{1}+1,f_{2}+1,\ldots,f_{m}+1)),

[move-2] (d,e,f)↦(d+fm,(e1+1,e2+1,…,en+1),(fm+n,f1,f2,…,fm−1)).(d,e,f)\mapsto(d+f_{m},(e_{1}+1,e_{2}+1,\ldots,e_{n}+1),(f_{m}+n,f_{1},f_{2},\ldots,f_{m-1})).

Lemma 2.5.

Any fixed Hanany-Witten equivalence class of brane diagrams contains infinitely many standard diagrams. The corresponding triples (d,e,f)(d,e,f) can be obtained from each other by a sequence of [move-1], [move-2] and their inverses.

Proof.

Take E1E_{1} and move it through consecutively the NS5 branes with HW transformations. Eventually, it will arrive to the left of F1F_{1}, so it can be moved on the bottom arc to the right of EnE_{n}. This yields [move-1]. When moving FmF_{m} consecutively through the D5 branes we get [move-2]. ∎

Example 2.6.

The two brane diagrams at the end of Section 2.1 are in standard form, and they are Hanany-Witten equivalent.

Example 2.7.

The m=n=1m=n=1 case is already interesting. Using the moves above (that is, Hanany-Witten transitions), the general standard form (d,(k),(k))(d,(k),(k)) can be brought to the form (d′,(0),(0))(d^{\prime},(0),(0)). The bow variety associated to the latter is (ℂ2)[d′]({\mathbb{C}}^{2})^{[d^{\prime}]}, the Hilbert scheme of d′d^{\prime} points on ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2}. Easy calculation gives d′=d−k⁡(k−1)/2d^{\prime}=d-k(k-1)/2.

3. Torus action

In Section 2.2 we indicated the action of the torus (ℂ∗)2=ℂt1∗×ℂt2∗({\mathbb{C}}^{*})^{2}={\mathbb{C}}^{*}_{t_{1}}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*}_{t_{2}} on 𝕄\mathbb{M} and ℕ\mathbb{N}. It is straightforward to verify that the map μ\mu is equivariant, and hence we obtain a ℂt1∗×ℂt2∗{\mathbb{C}}^{*}_{t_{1}}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*}_{t_{2}}-action on the bow variety. Moreover, the group (ℂ∗)n({\mathbb{C}}^{*})^{n} of linear reparametrizations of the lines ℂE{\mathbb{C}}_{E} also acts on the bow variety, and in turn, we have an action of

T=(ℂt1∗×ℂt2∗)×(ℂ∗)D5 branes=(ℂ∗)2×(ℂ∗)n=(ℂ∗)n+2.T=({\mathbb{C}}^{*}_{t_{1}}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*}_{t_{2}})\times({\mathbb{C}}^{*})^{\text{D5 branes}}=({\mathbb{C}}^{*})^{2}\times({\mathbb{C}}^{*})^{n}=({\mathbb{C}}^{*})^{n+2}.

3.2. Torus fixed points

The action of TT has isolated fixed points in ℳ\mathcal{M}. These fixed points ℳT\mathcal{M}^{T} can be described combinatorially in various ways. One description is via (generalized) Maya diagrams [17, Appendix A] (cf. [21, Appendix]) that we recall now.

By [18, Section 6.9.2] there exists a set of coordinates s1,…,sns_{1},\dots,s_{n} on (ℂ∗)n⊂T(\mathbb{C}^{\ast})^{n}\subset T such that the action on ℂi{\mathbb{C}}_{i} is induced by ui≔s1​…​siu_{i}\coloneqq s_{1}\dots s_{i} for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. Consider a representative (A,B,a,b,C,D)(A,B,a,b,C,D) of a point in ℳT\mathcal{M}^{T}. Then there must exist a homomorphism ρ:T→𝒢\rho:T\to\mathcal{G} such that

s1​…​sn​A1=ρE−​(t)−1​A1​ρE+​(t)s_{1}\dots s_{n}A_{1}=\rho_{E^{-}}(t)^{-1}A_{1}\rho_{E^{+}}(t)
AE=ρE−​(t)−1​AE​ρE+​(t),E≠E1A_{E}=\rho_{E^{-}}(t)^{-1}A_{E}\rho_{E^{+}}(t),\quad E\neq E_{1}

t1​t2​(s1​…​si)​bE=bE​ρE−​(t),E≠E1t_{1}t_{2}(s_{1}\dots s_{i})b_{E}=b_{E}\rho_{E^{-}}(t),\quad E\neq E_{1}
t1​CF=ρF−​(t)−1​CF​ρF+​(t)t_{1}C_{F}=\rho_{F^{-}}(t)^{-1}C_{F}\rho_{F^{+}}(t)
t2​DF=ρF+​(t)−1​DF​ρF−​(t)t_{2}D_{F}=\rho_{F^{+}}(t)^{-1}D_{F}\rho_{F^{-}}(t)

The space

V=⨁X​D3VXV=\bigoplus_{X\;\mathrm{D3}}V_{X}

decomposes into weight spaces with respect to ρ\rho:

V=⨁V⁡(t1,t2,s1,…,sn).V=\bigoplus V(t_{1},t_{2},s_{1},\dots,s_{n}).

By the above, AEA_{E}, E≠E1E\neq E_{1} preserves the (t,s)(t,s)-weight, A1A_{1} shifts the ss-weights by (−1,…,−1)(-1,\dots,-1), BXB_{X} preserves the ss-weight and decreases the tt-weight by (1,1)(1,1), aia_{i} sends ℂi\mathbb{C}_{i} to the weight space s1​…​sis_{1}\dots s_{i} (every other weight is 0), and bib_{i} is zero on every weight space other than t1t2(s1⋯si)t_{1}t_{2}(s_{1}\cdots s_{i}).

For 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, set

Vi=⨁Vi​(t1,t2)V^{i}=\bigoplus V^{i}(t_{1},t_{2})

where

Vi(t1,t2)=⊕k∈ℤV(t1,t2,s11+k,…,si1+k,si+1k,…,snk).V^{i}(t_{1},t_{2})=\oplus_{k\in{\mathbb{Z}}}V(t_{1},t_{2},s_{1}^{1+k},\dots,s_{i}^{1+k},s_{i+1}^{k},\dots,s_{n}^{k}).

Then ViV^{i} is a T2T^{2}-module and

V=⊕1≤i≤nVi.V=\oplus_{1\leq i\leq n}V^{i}.

By the above, ℂi\mathbb{C}_{i} can only interact with ViV^{i}, and hence the six-tuple (A,B,a,b,C,D)(A,B,a,b,C,D) also decomposes into a direct sum.

Let us restrict our attention on a single summand ViV^{i}. As aja_{j}, bjb_{j} are zero for j≠ij\neq i, AjA_{j} is an isomorphism due to stability conditions (S1)–(S2). Therefore, we can identify Vj−V_{j^{-}} with Vj+V_{j^{+}}, and the datum can be represented by a bow diagram with only one D5 brane. Instead of drawing this diagram on the cycle, we draw it on the universal cover, that is, a periodic brane on the infinte line. The D5 branes (all mapping onto EiE_{i} under the exponential map) appear at, let’s say, integer positions. The NS5 branes come in groups; these are called blocks and their positions are indexed by half-integers. This bow diagram and its block decomposition is compatible with the weight decomposition of the underlying vector spaces, because the map A1A_{1} shifts the ss-weights by (−1,…,−1)(-1,\dots,-1), while AiA_{i}, i≠1i\neq 1 preserves the weights.

3.3. Combinatorial codes of torus fixed points—Maya diagrams

We associate a 01 sequence to each D5 brane EiE_{i}. It follows from the stability conditions that (when restricted to ViV^{i}) the maps DjD_{j} that appear in the NS5 branes left (resp. right) of EiE_{i} are all injective (resp. surjective) and the dimension of the underlying spaces at consecutive D​3D3 branes is either constant or increases (resp. decreases) by 1. Take the 01 sequence where for negative (resp. positive) blocks 1 (resp. 0) indicates the places where the dimension increases (resp. decreases) and 0 (resp. 1) occurring at the places where the dimension is constant. Although ViV^{i} is finite dimensional, extend the sequence obtained this way by 0’s on the left and by 1’s on the right to get a sequence MiM_{i} infinite in both directions.

The (generalized) Maya diagram of the fixed point is obtained by placing the 01 sequence MiM_{i} for each 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n under each other. These Maya diagrams hence comprise sequences of 01 matrices of size n×mn\times m, again numbered with half integers.

  1. (i)

    For large enough kk all entries of block k2\frac{k}{2} are 1, and all entries of block −k2\frac{-k}{2} are 0.

  2. (ii)

    For 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n the entries satisfy

    ei=#⁡{0s in row ​i​ of positive blocks}−#⁡{1s in row ​i​ of negative blocks}.e_{i}=\#\{\textrm{0s in row }i\textrm{ of positive blocks}\}-\#\{\textrm{1s in row }i\textrm{ of negative blocks}\}.
  3. (iii)

    For 1≤j≤m1\leq j\leq m the entries satisfy

    fj=#⁡{0s in column ​Fj​ of positive blocks}−#⁡{1s in column ​Fj​ of negative blocks}.\ \hskip 22.76228ptf_{j}=\#\{\textrm{0s in column }F_{j}\textrm{ of positive blocks}\}\\ -\#\{\textrm{1s in column }F_{j}\textrm{ of negative blocks}\}.\hskip 22.76228pt\
  4. (iv)
    d=\displaystyle d= #⁡{1s in block ​−12}+2​#​{1s in block ​−32}+3​#​{1s in block ​−52}+…\displaystyle\#\{\textrm{1s in block }\frac{-1}{2}\}+2\#\{\textrm{1s in block }\frac{-3}{2}\}+3\#\{\textrm{1s in block }\frac{-5}{2}\}+\dots
    +#⁡{0s in block ​32}+2​#​{0s in block ​52}+3​#​{0s in block ​72}+….\displaystyle+\#\{\textrm{0s in block }\frac{3}{2}\}+2\#\{\textrm{0s in block }\frac{5}{2}\}+3\#\{\textrm{0s in block }\frac{7}{2}\}+\dots.

For a pair of integer vectors (e,f)∈ℤn×ℤm(e,f)\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}\times{\mathbb{Z}}^{m} and a nonnegative integer d∈ℤ≥0+d\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}^{+} let M⁡(d,e,f)M(d,e,f) be the set of Maya diagrams associated with fixed points on the bow variety ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}(d,e,f). Define

M⁡(e,f)=⨆d≥0M⁡(d,e,f).M(e,f)=\bigsqcup_{d\geq 0}M(d,e,f).

3.4. Combinatorial codes of torus fixed points—tie diagrams

There is another combinatorial code for torus fixed points, besides Maya diagrams: tie diagrams. They are closer to the physical origin of brane configurations. In tie diagrams D3 branes are realized by a number of ties, on each interval between 5-branes as many ties as the D3 multiplicity is there. A tie connects an NS5 brane to a D5 brane and goes along the circle of our diagram certain number of times. A tie diagram can have 0 or 1 tie for each triple (NS5 brane, D5 brane, winding number). In Figure 1 we illustrate a tie diagram of a torus fixed point, whose Maya diagram is

The correspondence between tie diagrams and Maya diagrams is as follows. Consider the universal cover of the tie diagram with the choice that all ties are lifted to a representative corresponding to a distinguished ‘block’ of D5 branes (see Figure 1). Then the possible ties from this group to groups of lifted NS5 branes come in blocks. These blocks correspond to the blocks of the Maya diagrams. For positive blocks (ties to the right) the rule is: the (E,F)(E,F) entry is 0 if there is a EE-FF tie, otherwise it is 1; and for negative blocks (ties to the left) the rule is: the (E,F)(E,F) entry is 1 if there is a EE-FF tie, otherwise it is 0. For more details see [21, Appendix].

If we replace such a picture with the picture on the right, we arrive at a combinatorial code called framed quiver of type A^\hat{A}. The geometric significance is that bow varieties associated with co-balanced brane diagrams are Nakajima quiver varieties associated with the quiver obtained this way [18]. Hence we will study which brane diagrams are Hanany-Witten equivalent to a co-balanced one.

Theorem 4.1.
  1. (1)

    A standard brane diagram of type (d,e,f)(d,e,f) is Hanany-Witten equivalent to a co-balanced diagram if and only if ee is an mm-bounded non-decreasing integer sequence, that is, if it satisfies ei∈ℤe_{i}\in{\mathbb{Z}},

    e1≤e2≤e3≤…≤en−1≤en≤e1+m.e_{1}\leq e_{2}\leq e_{3}\leq\ldots\leq e_{n-1}\leq e_{n}\ \leq e_{1}+m.
  2. (2)

Remark 4.2.

It is obvious from the definitions of [move-1] and [move-2] that the condition ee is an mm-bounded non-decreasing integer sequence is invariant under these moves.

Proof.

If ee is an mm-bounded non-decreasing integer sequence, then repeated applications of [move-1] or its inverse bring it to the form in Part (2), proving Part (2).

Consider the standard (d′,e′,f′)(d^{\prime},e^{\prime},f^{\prime}) brane diagram. Let us move E1E_{1} through −e1-e_{1} NS5 branes to the left, using HW transitions. Then let us move E2E_{2} through −e2-e_{2} NS5 branes to the left, using HW transitions, etc. What we obtain is exactly the brane diagram version of the quiver in Part (3). This proves that if ee is an mm-bounded non-decreasing integer sequence, then the (d,e,f)(d,e,f) standard diagram is HW equivalent to the quiver in the figure.

To prove the converse statement, let us consider the brane diagram version of the quiver above. The inverse of the HW transitions described above brings it to a standard form (d′,e′,f′)(d^{\prime},e^{\prime},f^{\prime}) satisfying the condition in Part (2). Remark 4.2 completes the proof. ∎

Example 4.3.

Consider the brane diagram in standard form with d=8d=8, e=(−1,−1,0CLOSE,e=(-1,-1,0, 0,0, OPEN1,1,2)1,1,2), f=(−4,4,2)f=(-4,4,2). It is Hanany-Witten equivalent (using three inverse [move-1]’s) to d=13d=13, e′=(−2,−2,−1,−1,−1,0,0)e^{\prime}=(-2,-2,-1,-1,-1,0,0), f′=(−7,1,−1)f^{\prime}=(-7,1,-1). In turn, the associated bow variety is a quiver variety of type A^\hat{A} with dimension vector (13,12,6)(13,12,6) and framing vector (2,3,2)(2,3,2).

4.2. D5 swaps

Definition 4.4.

Assume d2+d2′=d1+d3d_{2}+d^{\prime}_{2}=d_{1}+d_{3}. Carrying out the local change

(1)

in a brane diagram is called a D5 swap.

Lemma 4.5.

For a brane diagram in standard (d,e,f)(d,e,f) form swapping the D5 branes EiE_{i} and Ei+1E_{i+1} is the same as exchanging eie_{i} with ei+1e_{i+1} in ee while keeping dd and ff fixed.

Proof.

Follows from the construction. ∎

When we carry out a D5 swap on a brane diagram, the associated bow variety changes in general, even its dimension may change. In some examples the change is a homotopy equivalence (eg. one is the total space of a vector bundle with base space the other), but in other examples the cohomology ring changes considerably [11].

Let XX and X′X^{\prime} be the bow varieties associated to the diagrams on the left and right of (1). As already observed in [21, Section 8] there is a natural bijection between the torus fixed points of XX and X′X^{\prime}. The bijection on tie diagrams is depicted in Figure 2.

Hence, when counting torus fixed points for a (d,e,f)(d,e,f) diagram, we are allowed to carry out [move-1], [move-2], as well as permuting the components of ee. In particular, Theorem 4.1 implies that for any bow variety there is a quiver variety whose torus fixed point count is the same.

In Section 6.4 we will present a more refined analysis of the effect of D5 swap on the brane diagram.

Remark 4.6.

The torus fixed point count is also invariant under the analogous NS5 brane swaps [21, Section 8]—imagine Figure 2 upside down. The brane diagrams of quiver varieties with w=(2,3,2)w=(2,3,2) and vv being one of (10,7,3),(10,9,3),(2,7,3),(2,1,3),(4,9,3),(4,1,3)(10,7,3),(10,9,3),(2,7,3),(2,1,3),(4,9,3),(4,1,3) can be achieved from each other by HW transitions and NS5 brane swaps. Hence the fixed point count of these quiver varieties are the same.

5. Generating series and core-quotient decomposition

Recall that ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}(d,e,f) denotes the bow variety associated with the brane diagram in standard (d,e,f)(d,e,f) form.

Denote by K0​(V​a​r)K_{0}(Var) the Grothendieck ring of varieties over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, and let qq be a formal variable. Consider the generating series of the classes of the bow varieties for various values of dd:

𝒵⁡(q)=𝒵e,f​(q)=∑d≥0[ℳ⁡(d,e,f)]​qd∈K0​(V​a​r)​⟦q⟧.{\mathcal{Z}}(q)={\mathcal{Z}}_{e,f}(q)=\sum_{d\geq 0}[\mathcal{M}(d,e,f)]q^{d}\in K_{0}(Var)\llbracket q\rrbracket.
Remark 5.1.

In a similar manner, one could introduce a multivariable generating series

𝒵e,f(q−m+1,…,qn)=∑d≥0[ℳ(d,e,f)]q−m+1d−m+1⋯qndn{\mathcal{Z}}_{e,f}(q_{-m+1},\dots,q_{n})=\sum_{d\geq 0}[\mathcal{M}(d,e,f)]q_{-m+1}^{d_{-m+1}}\cdots q_{n}^{d_{n}}

with m+nm+n formal variables to keep track of all multiplicities. However, in this paper, we will not explore this multivariable version.

In enumerative problems one often considers a motivic measure, which is a ring homomorphism K0​(V​a​r)→RK_{0}(Var)\to R into a commutative ring RR. Some well-known examples of motivic measures include the Euler charactestic (with values in ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}), the virtual Poincaré polynomial (with values in the one-variable polynomial ring ℤ⁡[t]{\mathbb{Z}}[t]) and the E-polynomial (with values in the two-variable polynomial ring ℤ⁡[u,v]{\mathbb{Z}}[u,v]). A motivic measure ϕ\phi induces a ring homomorphism

ϕ:K0​(V​a​r)​⟦q⟧→R⁡⟦q⟧.\phi:K_{0}(Var)\llbracket q\rrbracket\to R\llbracket q\rrbracket.
Definition 5.2.

Let

Z⁡(q)=χ​(𝒵)​(q)=∑d≥0χ⁡(ℳ⁡(d,e,f))​qd∈ℤ​⟦q⟧,Z⁡(q,t)=Pt​(𝒵)​(q)=∑d≥0Pt​(ℳ⁡(d,e,f))​qd∈ℤ⁡[t]​⟦q⟧\begin{array}[]{rlll}Z(q)=&\chi({\mathcal{Z}})(q)=&\sum_{d\geq 0}\chi(\mathcal{M}(d,e,f))q^{d}&\in{\mathbb{Z}}\llbracket q\rrbracket,\\ Z(q,t)=&P_{t}({\mathcal{Z}})(q)=&\sum_{d\geq 0}P_{t}(\mathcal{M}(d,e,f))q^{d}&\in{\mathbb{Z}}[t]\llbracket q\rrbracket\end{array}

denote the generating series of the Euler numbers, and the generating series of the (virtual) Poincaré polynomials associated with the Borel-Moore homology.

In Section 7, we will derive closed formulas for 𝒵⁡(q){\mathcal{Z}}(q) and Z⁡(q,t)Z(q,t) in various cases. However, first, as warm-up, let us calculate Z⁡(q)Z(q) by introducing a core-quotient type combinatorial decomposition of generalized Maya diagrams.

Let MM be a Maya diagram, consisting of blocks Mb,b∈2​ℤ+12M^{b},b\in\frac{2{\mathbb{Z}}+1}{2}. Suppose that

Mi​jk2=1andMi​jk+22=0.M^{\frac{k}{2}}_{ij}=1\qquad\qquad\text{and}\qquad\qquad M^{\frac{k+2}{2}}_{ij}=0.

We obtain another Maya diagram if we replace the entry 1 by 0 and the entry 0 by 1 at the i​jij-positions of Mk2M^{\frac{k}{2}} and Mk+22M^{\frac{k+2}{2}}. When drawn on the n×∞n\times\infty matrix, this corresponds to shifting the 1 from Mi​jk2M^{\frac{k}{2}}_{ij} to the right while keeping its coordinate in the n×mn\times m arrangement. The core of a Maya diagram MM is the Maya diagram obtained from MM by successively shifting all 1’s to the right using such moves at all entries, until this is no longer possible at any entry.

Lemma 5.3.

Shifting a 1 right by one block has the following effects on the dimension vectors of the diagram:

  1. (1)

    ee does not change

  2. (2)

    ff does not change

  3. (3)

    dd decreases by 1

Proof.

This follows directly from properties (i)–(iv) of Maya diagrams (end of Section 3.3). ∎

We denote by C⁡(e,f)C(e,f) the set of (e,f)(e,f)-core diagrams, and by

core:M⁡(e,f)→C⁡(e,f)\mathrm{core}\colon M(e,f)\to C(e,f)

the map which takes an (e,f)(e,f)-diagram to its core.

In any (e,f)(e,f)-core there is a unique integer ci​jc_{ij} for each 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, 1≤j≤m1\leq j\leq m such that the leftmost 1 at the i​jij entry occurs in the block

2​ci​j+12∈2​ℤ+12.\frac{2c_{ij}+1}{2}\in\frac{2{\mathbb{Z}}+1}{2}.

We associate the integer matrix c=(ci​j)1≤i≤n, 1≤j≤mc=(c_{ij})_{1\leq i\leq n,\,1\leq j\leq m} with each core. We clearly have

∑j=1mci​j=ei,1≤i≤nand∑i=1mci​j=fj,1≤j≤m.\sum_{j=1}^{m}c_{ij}=e_{i},\quad 1\leq i\leq n\qquad\qquad\text{and}\qquad\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{m}c_{ij}=f_{j},\quad 1\leq j\leq m.

Lemma 5.5.

For the (e,f)(e,f)-core corresponding to the matrix (ci​j)(c_{ij}), we have

d=∑i,jci​j​(ci​j−1)2.d=\sum_{i,j}\frac{c_{ij}(c_{ij}-1)}{2}.
Proof.

Consider the contribution of the i​jij-entries to the expression for dd appearing in property (iv) above. For ci​j>0c_{ij}>0, the contribution is 1+2+…+(ci​j−1)=(ci​j2)1+2+\ldots+(c_{ij}-1)=\binom{c_{ij}}{2}. For ci​j≤0c_{ij}\leq 0, the contribution is 1+2+…+(−ci​j)=(−ci​j+12)=(ci​j2)1+2+\ldots+(-c_{ij})=\binom{-c_{ij}+1}{2}=\binom{c_{ij}}{2}. ∎

Lemma 5.6.

There is a bijection

M⁡(e,f)⟷C⁡(e,f)×Pn​mM(e,f)\longleftrightarrow C(e,f)\times P^{nm}

where PP is the set of partitions. (That is, Pn​mP^{nm} is the set of ordered n​mnm-tuples of partitions.)

Proof.

For any (e,f)(e,f)-diagram the positions of the 1’s at the i​jij-entries determine a partition: the leftmost 1 is shifted left from the leftmost 1 of its core by a nonnegative integer λ1\lambda_{1}, the second leftmost 1 is shifted left from the second leftmost 1 of its core by a nonnegative integer λ2≤λ1\lambda_{2}\leq\lambda_{1}, etc. ∎

Thus we obtain the following expression for Z⁡(q)=Ze,f​(q)=∑d≥0|M⁡(d,e,f)|​qdZ(q)=Z_{e,f}(q)=\sum_{d\geq 0}|M(d,e,f)|q^{d}.

Theorem 5.7.

Let e∈ℤne\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} and f∈ℤmf\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{m} be fixed vectors. Then

Z⁡(q)=(∑c∈ℤn​m∑jci​j=ei∑ici​j=fjq∑i,jci​j​(ci​j−1)/2)⏟Z0​(q)⋅∏l=1∞(11−ql)n​m.Z(q)=\underbrace{\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{nm}\\ \sum_{j}c_{ij}=e_{i}\\ \sum_{i}c_{ij}=f_{j}\end{subarray}}q^{\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}(c_{ij}-1)/2}\right)}_{Z_{0}(q)}\cdot\prod_{l=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{1-q^{l}}\right)^{nm}.

The summation runs for a translated lattice in ℝn​m{\mathbb{R}}^{nm}, with the qq-exponent being a quadratic function of the coordinates. Thus, the series can be viewed as translated lattice theta-function, that are expected to exhibit modular properties.

Example 5.8.

For e=(−1,1)e=(-1,1), f=(0,0)f=(0,0) the series in the large parentheses is

Z0​(q)=2​∑k=0∞q2​k​(k+1)+1Z_{0}(q)=2\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}q^{2k(k+1)+1}

and hence Z⁡(q)=2​q+8​q2+28​q3+80​q4+212​q5+512​q6+1176​q7+O⁡(q8)Z(q)=2q+8q^{2}+28q^{3}+80q^{4}+212q^{5}+512q^{6}+1176q^{7}+O(q^{8}).

Example 5.9.

For more interesting ee and ff vectors computer evidence suggests that we obtain series of number theoretical significance, consistent with physics expectations. Here are two examples.

  • •

    For e=f=(3,2,1)e=f=(3,2,1) the series in the large parentheses is

    By Theorem A.1, the coefficients are exactly σ⁡(3​n+1)\sigma(3n+1) (σ\sigma is the sum-of-divisors function). This series—up to a reparametrization—is a modular form for the congruence subgroup Γ0​(9)\Gamma_{0}(9) of weight 2 (cf. A144614 of [10]). The infinite product part is equal to q924​η​(q)−9q^{\frac{9}{24}}\eta(q)^{-9} where η⁡(q)=η⁡(e2​π​i​τ)\eta(q)=\eta(e^{2\pi i\tau}) is the Dedekind η\eta-function. Therefore, the series

    Z⁡(q)=1+16​q+125​q2+723​q3+3428​q4+14167​q5+52679​q6+O⁡(q7)Z(q)=1+16q+125q^{2}+723q^{3}+3428q^{4}+14167q^{5}+52679q^{6}+O(q^{7})

    is a meromorphic modular form.

  • •

    The e=(−1,−1,−1)e=(-1,-1,-1), f=(−2,−1,0)f=(-2,-1,0) example is similar: we have

    Z0​(q)=3​q3+6​q4+15​q5+12​q6+24​q7+18​q8+42​q9+24​q10+O⁡(q11)Z_{0}(q)=3q^{3}+6q^{4}+15q^{5}+12q^{6}+24q^{7}+18q^{8}+42q^{9}+24q^{10}+O(q^{11})

    whose coefficients are σ⁡(3​n+2)\sigma(3n+2).

Remark 5.10.

It is easy to verify that the effects of [D5-swap], [move-1], or [move-2] on the series Z⁡(q)Z(q) are inessential: Z⁡(q)Z(q) gets multiplied by a qq-power (q0q^{0}, qe1q^{e_{1}}, qfmq^{f_{m}}, respectively).

Remark 5.11.

If e=(0,…,0)e=(0,\ldots,0) then ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}(d,e,f) is a quiver variety of affine type A such that the framing vector has one non-0 component. Various formulas are know for Z⁡(q)Z(q) in this case. For example, consider one more summation over the possible dimension vectors ff

∑f∈ℤm∑jfj=0∑c∈ℤn​m∑jci​j=0∑ici​j=fjq∑i,jci​j​(ci​j−1)/2.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}f\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{m}\\ \sum_{j}f_{j}=0\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{nm}\\ \sum_{j}c_{ij}=0\\ \sum_{i}c_{ij}=f_{j}\end{subarray}}q^{\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}(c_{ij}-1)/2}.

This is equal to

∑c∈ℤn​m∑jci​j=0q∑i,jci​j​(ci​j−1)/2=∑l∈ℤn⁡(m−1)q∑i=1n12​⟨li,li⟩Δ\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{nm}\\ \sum_{j}c_{ij}=0\end{subarray}}q^{\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}(c_{ij}-1)/2}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}l\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n(m-1)}\end{subarray}}q^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{2}\langle l_{i},l_{i}\rangle_{\Delta}}

where the inner product is taken with respect to the Cartan matrix of finite type Am−1A_{m-1}; see eg. [8, Section 3], cf. [7, Corollary 4.12].

Recall that T=ℂt1∗×ℂt2∗×(ℂ∗)D5 branesT={\mathbb{C}}^{*}_{t_{1}}\times{\mathbb{C}}^{*}_{t_{2}}\times\left({\mathbb{C}}^{*}\right)^{\text{D5 branes}}, and correspondingly, we have

6.2. Combinatorial codes of torus fixed points—extended Young diagrams

We continue to assume that there are nn D5 branes and mm NS5 branes. In this section we present yet another description of torus fixed points of bow varieties, which will be useful in some of our calculations.

Let M=(M1,…,Mn)M=(M_{1},\dots,M_{n}) be a generalized Maya diagram with component MiM_{i} corresponding to the D5 brane EiE_{i}. We can represent each row MiM_{i} with a Young diagram type picture. Consider the set ℤ×ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}\times{\mathbb{Z}} of integer pairs, which we will visualize as a set of blocks on the plane rotated by 4545 degrees. Specifically, axis for the t1t_{1}-weight runs from top left to bottom right, while the axis for the t2t_{2}-weight runs from top right to bottom left.

Since we are only considering integer coordinates, vertical lines are of the form (a−b)modm≡j(a-b)\mod m\equiv j. Blocks along the line (a−b)modm≡0(a-b)\mod m\equiv 0 will be further divided into two triangles vertically. In each such block the left half is labelled 0 while the right half is labelled 1. The remaining blocks are labelled vertically with m−1m-1 labels 2,…,m2,\ldots,m as shown in the picture: the block at position (i,j)(i,j) is labelled with (a−b)+1modm(a-b)+1\mod m.

For example, the labeling in the top quadrant looks as follows:

This diagonal labeling (or coloring) is a modification of the pattern of affine type A^\hat{A} [8]. When drawing a diagram, we understand that its boxes are colored (labelled) according to the above pattern.

In the classical Young diagram literature the number eie_{i} is called the charge of MiM_{i}. When ei=0e_{i}=0 there is a well defined Am−1A_{m-1}-colored Young diagram corresponding to MiM_{i}; see e.g. [15, Section 2.5] or [7, Section 2.3]. We generalise this to to cases where eie_{i} is arbitrary. Set the base level of our diagram to the line y=eiy=e_{i} (recall that the picture is rotated by 45 degrees):
ei<0e_{i}<0 ei=0e_{i}=0 ei>0e_{i}>0

The diagram representing MiM_{i} is drawn as follows:

  • •

    Extend this with the triangle

    (4) Ti=Tei≔{(0,0)​–​(ei+1,0)​–​(ei+1,ei+1)ifei<0,(1,1)​–​(ei,1)​–​(ei,ei)ifei>0.T_{i}=T_{e_{i}}\coloneqq\begin{cases}(0,0)\text{--}(e_{i}+1,0)\text{--}(e_{i}+1,e_{i}+1)&\quad\text{if}\quad e_{i}<0,\\ (1,1)\text{--}(e_{i},1)\text{--}(e_{i},e_{i})&\quad\text{if}\quad e_{i}>0.\end{cases}

6.3. Torus characters of the tangent space

6.3.1. Case of one NS5 brane

In this section, we assume m=1m=1. We have observed that if the charge eie_{i} of the row MiM_{i} of a Maya diagram is zero, the corresponding extended Young diagram is just a standard Young diagram. When all ei=0e_{i}=0, then the bow variety becomes a quiver variety. We will reduce the computation of the characters for an arbitrary extended Young diagram inductively to this quivers case by gradually decreasing ∑i|ei|\sum_{i}|e_{i}| until it reaches zero.

If the charge ei<0e_{i}<0, we can write an extended Young diagram BiB_{i} as

where B¯i\overline{B}_{i} is an extended Young diagram with charge e¯i=ei+1\overline{e}_{i}=e_{i}+1. Then Yi=(−1,0)⋅Y¯iY_{i}=(-1,0)\cdot\overline{Y}_{i} for the Young diagram parts, and the monomials

L0=1+⋯+t1ei+1​t2ei+1L_{0}=1+\dots+t_{1}^{e_{i}+1}t_{2}^{e_{i}+1}

resp.

span the half-boxes which were deleted from BiB_{i}. Similarly, if ei>0e_{i}>0, write BiB_{i} as

where B¯\overline{B} is an extended Young diagram with charge e¯i=ei−1\overline{e}_{i}=e_{i}-1. In this case Yi=(1,0)⋅Y¯iY_{i}=(1,0)\cdot\overline{Y}_{i}, and the monomials

L1=t1​t2+⋯+t1ei​t2eiL_{1}=t_{1}t_{2}+\dots+t_{1}^{e_{i}}t_{2}^{e_{i}}

resp.

L0=t1​(t1​t2+⋯+t1ei−1​t2ei−1)L_{0}=t_{1}(t_{1}t_{2}+\dots+t_{1}^{e_{i}-1}t_{2}^{e_{i}-1})

span the half-boxes removed from BiB_{i}.

Fix 1≤α,β≤n1\leq\alpha,\beta\leq n with diagrams Bα=Yα+TαB_{\alpha}=Y_{\alpha}+T_{\alpha} and Bβ=Yβ+TβB_{\beta}=Y_{\beta}+T_{\beta}. Denote by

the contribution of the pair (Bα,Bβ)(B_{\alpha},B_{\beta}) to the character in Corollary 6.1. Denote by Nα¯,β​(t1,t2)N_{\overline{\alpha},\beta}(t_{1},t_{2}), resp. Nα,β¯​(t1,t2)N_{\alpha,\overline{\beta}}(t_{1},t_{2}) the same quotient for the pair (B¯α,Bβ)(\overline{B}_{\alpha},B_{\beta}), resp. (Bα,B¯β)(B_{\alpha},\overline{B}_{\beta}).

6.3.2. General case

Recall that a Maya diagram MM has blocks

k=…,−3/2,−1/2,1/2,3/2,…,k=\ldots,-3/2,-1/2,1/2,3/2,\ldots,

and each block is an n×mn\times m matrix, where nn is the number of D5 branes and mm is the number of NS5 branes. Denote the (Ei,Fj)(E_{i},F_{j}) entry of the block kk by Mi,jkM^{k}_{i,j}.

Definition 6.6.

For an entry (Ei,Fj)(E_{i},F_{j}) in the block kk of a Maya diagram define sk,i,js_{k,i,j} to be the sum of all the entries left of this entry (including this entry). That is,

sk,i,j=∑l=−∞k−1∑a=1mMi,al+∑a=1jMi,ak.s_{k,i,j}=\sum_{l=-\infty}^{k-1}\sum_{a=1}^{m}M^{l}_{i,a}+\sum_{a=1}^{j}M^{k}_{i,a}.

This number is well defined because the Maya diagram is ‘eventually 0’ to the left.

Definition 6.7.

A 01-pair for a Maya diagram is

  • •

    an entry 1 in block k1k_{1} at position (Ei1,Fj)(E_{i_{1}},F_{j}), and

  • •

    an entry 0 in block k0k_{0} at position (Ei0,Fj)(E_{i_{0}},F_{j}),

if either k0>k1k_{0}>k_{1} or (k0=k1k_{0}=k_{1} and i0<i1i_{0}<i_{1}).

For a 01-pair let s1s_{1} be sk,i,js_{k,i,j} corresponding to the “1” in the pair and let k1k_{1} be the block number of the “1” in the pair. Similarly, let s0s_{0} be sk,i,js_{k,i,j} corresponding to the “0” in the pair and let k0k_{0} be the block number of the “0” in the pair.

Theorem 6.8.

The Maya diagram MM represents a torus fixed point in the bow variety. At this point the tangent space to the bow variety, in torus equivariant K-theory is equal to

(7) ∑01-pairs(ui0ui1​t1s1−s0+m⁡(k0−k1)​t2s1−s0+ui1ui0​t11−s1+s0−m⁡(k0−k1)​t21−s1+s0)\sum_{\text{01-pairs}}\left(\frac{u_{i_{0}}}{u_{i_{1}}}t_{1}^{s_{1}-s_{0}+m(k_{0}-k_{1})}t_{2}^{s_{1}-s_{0}}+\frac{u_{i_{1}}}{u_{i_{0}}}t_{1}^{1-s_{1}+s_{0}-m(k_{0}-k_{1})}t_{2}^{1-s_{1}+s_{0}}\right)
Proof.

The proof of [6, Theorem 3.2] generalizes from the type A case to the type A^\hat{A} case. For this, note that a tie diagram of type A^\hat{A} determines a tie diagram of type AA if we cut off the irrelevant parts outside of the ties. This is equivalent with forgetting the irrelevant part of the Maya diagram; the process is compatible with the dimension of the spaces VjV_{j} and hence with those of the tangent spaces due to the construction of the Maya diagram. By the block periodicity in the affine case we have to add m⁡(k0−k1)m(k_{0}-k_{1}) to the t1t_{1}-exponent s1−s0s_{1}-s_{0}. Note also that the four elementary diagram pieces in [6, Page 11] can be endowed with our (ℂ∗)2(\mathbb{C}^{\ast})^{2}-action in a compatible manner and this action carries through the whole proof. ∎

Theorem 6.10.

and Rα,βeα,eβR_{\alpha,\beta}^{e_{\alpha},e_{\beta}} is defined in (6).

Proof.

By forgetting the ℤ/m​ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}/m{\mathbb{Z}} equivariant structure we can consider the Maya diagram MM as a Maya diagram M′M^{\prime} of a fixed point of a bow variety with a single NS5 brane. 6.4. The effect of D5 swap

Let us consider again the combinatorial operation called D5 swap depicted in (1); for simplicity we will restrict our attention to separated brane diagrams. The associated bow varieties will be called ℳ=ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}(d,e,f) and ℳ′=ℳ⁡(d,e′,f)\mathcal{M}^{\prime}=\mathcal{M}(d,e^{\prime},f) respectively. The vector e′e^{\prime} is obtained from ee by swapping the jj’th and j+1j+1’st components, where EjE_{j} and Ej+1E_{j+1} are the two swapped D5 branes.

Let x∈ℳ⁡(d,e,f)x\in\mathcal{M}(d,e,f) and x′∈ℳ⁡(d,e′,f)x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}(d,e^{\prime},f) be torus fixed points in the two varieties, corresponding to each other under the bijection illustrated in Figure 2. The Maya diagram of x′x^{\prime} is obtained from the Maya diagram of xx by swapping the jj’th and j+1j+1’st rows.

W={−uj+1uj∑i=1Δ(t1t2)iif ​Δ≥0uj+1uj​∑i=Δ+10(t1​t2)iif ​Δ<0.W=\begin{cases}-\frac{u_{j+1}}{u_{j}}\sum_{i=1}^{\Delta}(t_{1}t_{2})^{i}&\text{if }\Delta\geq 0\\ \phantom{-}\frac{u_{j+1}}{u_{j}}\sum_{i=\Delta+1}^{0}(t_{1}t_{2})^{i}&\text{if }\Delta<0.\end{cases}

For k≪0k\ll 0 this statement is vacuously true, and the k→k+1k\to k+1 induction step follows (in the four possible [00]\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 0\end{bmatrix}, [10]\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}, [01]\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 1\end{bmatrix}, [11]\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 1\end{bmatrix} cases) from the formula in Theorem 6.8.

It remains to prove that Δ\Delta in a column far right is equal to ej+1−eje_{j+1}-e_{j}. For this let l1,l2,l3l_{1},l_{2},l_{3} denote the number of [11]\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 1\end{bmatrix}, [10]\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}, [01]\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 1\end{bmatrix} occurrences in rows jj and j+1j+1 in negative blocks. Let r1,r2,r3r_{1},r_{2},r_{3} denote the number of [10]\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}, [01]\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 1\end{bmatrix}, [00]\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 0\end{bmatrix} occurrences in rows jj and j+1j+1 in positive blocks. Then we have that Δ\Delta on the far right is equal to

(l2+r1)−(l3+r2)=((r1+r3)−(l1+l3))−((r2+r3)−(l1+l2))=ej+1−ej,(l_{2}+r_{1})-(l_{3}+r_{2})=\left((r_{1}+r_{3})-(l_{1}+l_{3})\right)-\left((r_{2}+r_{3})-(l_{1}+l_{2})\right)=e_{j+1}-e_{j},

which completes the proof. ∎

A remarkable consequence of Theorem 6.11 is that the difference (8) only depends on the ambient variety ℳ\mathcal{M}, not on the fixed point x∈ℳx\in\mathcal{M}. There could be a simple geometric explanation for this phenomenon: specifically, if ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} were the total space of a vector bundle over ℳ\mathcal{M} (with a TT action), or vice versa. Indeed, in many examples this is the case—one of ℳ\mathcal{M} or ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} is a vector bundle over the other. However, this is not always true; a counterexample is provided in [11], where one of the varieties is a point, and the other has odd cohomology.

Although our desire for ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} to be a vector bundle over ℳ\mathcal{M} (or vice versa) is not strictly accurate, Theorem 6.11 demonstrates that near the torus fixed points, they resemble a situation where one is a vector bundle over the other.

Let x∈ℳx\in\mathcal{M} be a fixed point of the TT-action. Then Tx​ℳT_{x}\mathcal{M} has a TT-module structure, and has an induced ℂ∗\mathbb{C}^{\ast}-module structure via γ\gamma. We calculate the sum of dimensions of weight spaces with the above condition in each summand of Theorem 6.10 separately, and then sum up the contribution from each summand. In the summand α=β\alpha=\beta, the contribution is

|Yα|−l⁡(Yα)|Y_{\alpha}|-l(Y_{\alpha})

where the binomial term is understood to be zero if eβ−eα−1≤0e_{\beta}-e_{\alpha}-1\leq 0. If α>β\alpha>\beta, the above condition is equivalent to that the weight of t2t_{2} is negative. The contribution is hence

7.5. Cell decomposition

We now give a sufficient condition for the Białynicki-Birula cells to cover the bow variety ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}(d,e,f). We continue using the one-parameter subgroup γ\gamma specified in (10).

Theorem 7.17.

Assume that e∈ℤne\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} is an m+1m+1-bounded non-decreasing sequence, that is

(11) e1≤e2≤⋯≤en≤e1+m+1.e_{1}\leq e_{2}\leq\dots\leq e_{n}\leq e_{1}+m+1.

Then (9) holds for ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}(d,e,f). In particular, Proposition 7.1 and Corollary 7.2 hold for any dd and ff.

For quiver varieties ee is an mm-bounded non-decreasing sequence, which implies m+1m+1-boundedness. Hence Theorem 7.17 extends well-known properties of quiver varieties to a larger class of bow varieties.

Remark 7.18.

For our specific choice of the one-parameter subgroup γ\gamma, computer evidence suggests that (11) is not only sufficient but also necessary for (9) to hold for all f∈ℤmf\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{m} and dd.

Proof of Theorem 7.17.

We will use Theorem 6.10; denote the two terms of Nα,βN_{\alpha,\beta} in it by QQ and RR respectively. By the same considerations as in the proof of Theorem 7.5, the dimension of a (+)(+)-cell depends on the number summands in Nα,βN_{\alpha,\beta} such that the weight of t2t_{2} is positive, resp. nonnegative when α<β\alpha<\beta, resp. α>β\alpha>\beta, while it is independent from the components of ee when α=β\alpha=\beta.

Recall that if e1=⋯=en=0e_{1}=\dots=e_{n}=0, then the bow variety directly corresponds to a quiver variety. It is known that quiver varieties of affine type A always have a maximal dimensional cell [16, 7]. Note as well that the shift t1eβ−eαt_{1}^{e_{\beta}-e_{\alpha}} in the QQ-term of Nα,βN_{\alpha,\beta} does not change the t2t_{2}-weights of the summands. Combining these facts, we get that for any bow variety there exists a fixed point for which all the QQ-terms lie in the positive weight space for our choice of the one-parameter subgroup γ\gamma.

Our assumption assures that

0\displaystyle 0 ≤eβ−eα\displaystyle\leq e_{\beta}-e_{\alpha} if ​α≤β\displaystyle\quad\textrm{if }\alpha\leq\beta
−m−1\displaystyle-m-1 ≤eβ−eα\displaystyle\leq e_{\beta}-e_{\alpha} if ​α>β\displaystyle\quad\textrm{if }\alpha>\beta

for all 1≤α,β≤n1\leq\alpha,\beta\leq n. By definitions (6) and (4), these imply that all terms in Rα,βeα,eβR_{\alpha,\beta}^{e_{\alpha},e_{\beta}} have positive, resp. nonnegative t2t_{2}-weight when α<β\alpha<\beta, resp. α>β\alpha>\beta.

Combining all these, we get that for the specific fixed point obtained above both the QQ and RR terms lie in the positive weight space. So the corresponding cell is maximal dimensional. In ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} the (+)(+)-set whence covers the whole variety, while the (−)(-)-set is a point.

∎

7.5.1. Quiver-like bow varieties

Observe that the favorable properties collected in Proposition 7.1 do not depend on the choice of the one-parameter subgroup γ\gamma. As long as a γ\gamma exists with property (9) we have the consequences of Proposition 7.1. A simple way of considering another γ\gamma for ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}(d,e,f) is carrying out a [move-1] on the triple (d,e,f)(d,e,f). Then the γ\gamma defined by (10) changes, because the torus gets reparametrized. Hence we obtain the following.

Corollary 7.19.

If repeated applications of [move-1]’s (or its inverse) can change (d,e,f)(d,e,f) to a triple (d′,e′,f′)(d^{\prime},e^{\prime},f^{\prime}) such that e′e^{\prime} is a m+1m+1-bounded non-decreasing sequence, then ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}(d,e,f) satisfies the properties listed in Proposition 7.1.

It is worth mentioning how to recognize vectors e∈ℤne\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} that are [move-1]-equivalent to a m+1m+1-bounded non-decreasing sequence. Define

δ1=e2−e1,δ2=e3−e2,…,δn−1=en−en−1,δn=(e1+m)−en.\delta_{1}=e_{2}-e_{1},\ \delta_{2}=e_{3}-e_{2},\ \ldots,\ \delta_{n-1}=e_{n}-e_{n-1},\ \delta_{n}=(e_{1}+m)-e_{n}.
Proposition 7.20.

A vector e∈ℤne\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} is [move-1]-equivalent to an m+1m+1-bounded non-decreasing sequence if and only if

(12) ∃j∈{1,…,n}:δj≥−1​ and ​(δi≥0​ for ​i≠j).\exists j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\qquad\delta_{j}\geq-1\text{ and }(\delta_{i}\geq 0\text{ for }i\not=j).
Proof.

Follows from the definition of [move-1]. ∎

This condition is a relaxation of the “all δi≥0\delta_{i}\geq 0” condition that would make the ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}(d,e,f) variety a quiver variety, cf. Theorem 4.1. Therefore the bow varieties ℳ⁡(d,e,f)\mathcal{M}(d,e,f) for which ee satisfies (12) can be considered quiver-like: they share the crucial properties collected in Proposition 7.1 with quiver varieties.

Corollary 8.3.

Let m=1m=1. Assume that e∈ℤne\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} is a 22-bounded non-decreasing sequence. Then for any d∈ℤ≥0d\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}

It would be exciting to construct a parabolic analogue of the moduli space of instantons on the blown-up plane and to investigate the counterpart of Nekrasov’s regularity conjecture. As bow varieties are expected to parameterise parabolic sheaves on the plane blown-up already in one point, the above spaces could be related in fact to sheaves on the plane blown-up in two points.

Beside observing their formal similarity, the precise relation between Z⁡(ε1,ε2,a,q)Z(\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2},a,q) and the partition function of the blown-up plane [20, (6.10)] is another intriguing question we leave for further investigation.
